strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and understudied gap: foundational time-series description as a prerequisite for complex temporal reasoning, with a clear analogy to arithmetic being foundational for math reasoning.

Comprehensive empirical scope: 17 models spanning LLMs, VLMs, and TSLMs across five datasets, three tasks, and multiple negative-sampling strategies, giving broad head-to-head comparisons that prior work largely lacks.

Includes a human evaluation using six criteria with high inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's Kappa and Krippendorff's Alpha > 0.8), and cross-validates rankings across three evaluation methods (DeBERTa NLI, GPT-5 judging, human annotation), which strengthens the generation-evaluation claims.

Non-obvious and useful findings: VLMs consistently outperform dedicated TSLMs and text-only LLMs, and all approaches are fragile under realistic perturbations, yielding actionable directions for the community.

Adds robustness testing (length, missingness, amplitude scaling, Gaussian noise, image quality, CoT) that goes beyond standard benchmark accuracy reporting, and a per-class complexity analysis on SUSHI.
Thorough appendix with negative-sampling ablations, refusal-rate diagnostics for ChatTime, and a transparent model-applicability analysis (Table 5) justifying which TSLMs could be evaluated.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and the 'first rigorous benchmark for automatically describing time series' claim is overstated given closely related benchmarks the authors themselves cite, notably CaTS-Bench ('Can language models describe numeric time series?') and TADACap, which target the same captioning/description goal. The paper reuses five existing datasets rather than creating new data, so the contribution is primarily unification plus empirical study.

The proposed tasks are relatively simple (True/False recognition and 4-way MCQ differentiation), and negative options are chosen as the 'most dissimilar' descriptions, which the authors admit provides an 'upper-bound estimate.' This eases the task and weakens the benchmark's discriminative power, evidenced by near-ceiling VLM accuracy on several datasets.

Generation evaluation is restricted to a single dataset (SUSHI), limiting generality of the generation conclusions, and the absolute NLI entailment numbers are very low (best bidirectional ~16%), which raises questions about whether the automated metric is measuring the intended quality rather than lexical/style mismatch.

Contradictory statements about artifact release: the introduction/contributions state code and data 'has been made public,' while the related-work section says they 'will release all code and data ... upon acceptance.' This inconsistency undermines reproducibility claims.

Presentation and reporting issues: Table 2a appears to have a malformed/merged Phi-3.5 row, Table 16 labels TSLMs as 'Tunics' and uses 'GPT-4ovLT,' and model names (GPT-5.4-mini, Gemini-3.0-flash) with 2026 access dates raise reproducibility/verifiability concerns for readers.

ChatTime is reported with below-random accuracy largely because of instruction-following/refusal failures rather than representational capability; although diagnosed in Appendix I, its inclusion in headline results could mislead readers about TSLM capability and biases the cross-modality narrative.

Robustness analysis is skewed: interpolation, missingness, amplitude, and noise are mainly reported for LLMs/TSLMs, with VLMs tested only for image-quality degradation, so the robustness claims for VLMs are less well supported than implied by the abstract's 'all approaches are clearly fragile.'

strengths: Timely and relevant topic: the paper targets an under-evaluated capability, automatic description of time-series structure, which is important for multimodal time-series-language models.

Unifies five public datasets into three tasks (recognition, differentiation, open generation) and supports three input modalities (text, plots, raw numeric vectors), enabling direct head-to-head comparison of LLMs, VLMs, and TSLMs.

Broad empirical study: evaluates 17 models, uses four negative-sampling strategies, reports automated NLI metrics, a GPT-5 judge, and a human evaluation, and includes several robustness tests (length, missingness, amplitude scaling, noise, image degradation, CoT prompting).
The robustness analyses provide useful diagnostic signals, especially the modality-dependent degradation under noise, missingness, and image-quality corruption.
Full appendix results, prompt templates, and a limitations section are included; code and data are promised to be released.

Some findings are useful for the community, such as the consistent advantage of VLM variants over their LLM counterparts and the observation that text-only prompting struggles on noisy real-world series.
weaknesses: The central benchmark design is too easy to support the claim that the tasks measure fundamental structural description. Negative examples are deliberately chosen to be maximally dissimilar, and the authors themselves describe this as an upper-bound setup. This allows models to solve recognition/differentiation using superficial cues rather than genuine time-series understanding, and there is no human ceiling or distractor-difficulty analysis.

Dataset composition undermines the general-purpose framing: NICU-HR alone contributes 36,679 of 46,843 pairs (~78%), and its descriptions are clinically event-specific (bradycardia, variability) rather than generic structural properties. The headline '90.44% real-world' is therefore dominated by one specialized dataset, which skews aggregate rankings and conclusions.

Open-generation evaluation is limited to SUSHI, a synthetic dataset, so no real-world generation capability is actually tested. Absolute NLI entailment rates are very low (e.g., 16.29% bidirectional for GPT-5.4-mini VLM), making it unclear whether any model generates correct descriptions. Human evaluation covers only three models and 340 samples.

The TSLM comparison is weak and potentially unfair. Only two TSLMs are evaluated, and one (ChatTime-7B) frequently refuses or fails instruction following (refusal rates up to 83.4%), yet it is still included in main comparisons. Many other TSLMs are excluded, so the broad claim that dedicated TSLMs 'fall short' is not well supported.

No simple baselines are reported, such as feature-based/statistical classifiers, trained plot classifiers, or fine-tuned TSLM baselines. Without them, it is unclear whether the tasks require multimodal reasoning or can be solved by trivial heuristics.

There is a representation confound: LLMs receive comma-separated numeric strings, VLMs receive plots, and TSLMs receive raw numeric vectors. The observed VLM advantage may reflect plot representation rather than modality superiority, and no control experiment (e.g., LLM with textual plot statistics or VLM with raw numbers) is provided.

Negative sampling and evaluation protocols are not fully controlled across datasets: Euclidean distance is excluded for TaxoSynth, class/subclass constraints are used for SUSHI/TaxoSynth, and NICU-HR distractors are constrained by mortality labels. This introduces possible label-related cues and prevents perfectly controlled cross-dataset comparisons.

Robustness results lack statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, random seeds, significance tests, or effect-size analysis are reported. The CoT gain is described as consistent but is only +0.03 on average, and explanations for model behavior (e.g., Qwen attention diffusion) are speculative and unsupported.

Reproducibility is concerning because several evaluated models are proprietary APIs (GPT-5.4-mini, Gemini-3.0-flash) that are non-deterministic and may change. Prompts are provided, but decoding parameters, seeds, model versions, and batching details are insufficient, and the promised code/data are not available for review.

Novelty and presentation are overstated: 'first rigorous benchmark' is questionable given concurrent benchmarks cited in the paper (e.g., CaTS-Bench, TADACap, Time-MQA), and the abstract's conclusion that TSLMs 'fall short' conflicts with results showing ChatTS-14B outperforms comparable LLMs on several datasets.

The foundational-task claim is asserted rather than validated. The analogy that description recognition is 'like addition for math reasoning' is not empirically tested, and there is no downstream correlation showing that BEDTime performance predicts performance on complex time-series reasoning tasks.

The human evaluation is limited: only 340 descriptions, 40 overlapping annotations, and three models. There is no human evaluation for recognition/differentiation, and the six criteria are adapted from prior work but not validated for this benchmark.

The impact statement dismisses societal consequences, but NICU-HR includes mortality labels and sensitive clinical signals. Privacy, data-use, and potential clinical deployment implications are not discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-evaluated problem: foundational time-series description capabilities that should underlie more complex multimodal time-series reasoning. BEDTime fills a real gap between simple numeric benchmarks and elaborate reasoning/QA benchmarks.

The benchmark is substantial and well constructed: five public datasets are unified into 46,843 time-series/description pairs, with three tasks (recognition, differentiation, open generation) and support for text, numeric, and image modalities.

The empirical study is broad and informative: 17 models across LLMs, VLMs, and TSLMs are compared head-to-head, with multiple negative-sampling strategies, per-class analysis, and six robustness perturbations covering length, missingness, amplitude scaling, noise, image degradation, and CoT prompting.

Generation evaluation is thoughtfully triangulated with DeBERTa NLI, GPT-5 judging, and human annotation; the reported ranking consistency across evaluators strengthens confidence in the relative model ordering.

The findings are actionable for the community: VLMs consistently beat their LLM counterparts, TSLMs are competitive but limited, and all model families show brittleness under realistic perturbations, pointing to concrete future directions.

Reproducibility and transparency are generally strong: prompts, sampling procedures, implementation details, and planned code/data release are documented, and the limitations section is honest about synthetic data, univariate scope, NLI sensitivity, and limited TSLM coverage.

No material ethical concerns are apparent: the work uses public or previously released datasets, includes an impact statement, and does not appear to introduce new privacy or misuse risks beyond those already present in time-series modeling.
weaknesses: Negative examples for recognition and differentiation are selected to be maximally dissimilar, which makes the tasks easier and may inflate absolute accuracy. Hard or adversarial negatives are not systematically included, so the benchmark may not fully isolate fine-grained structural understanding.

Open-ended generation is evaluated only on SUSHI, and the DeBERTa NLI entailment scores are low in absolute terms. Human evaluation covers only three models and a relatively small sample, so generation conclusions are less comprehensive than the recognition/differentiation results.

Conclusions about TSLMs are based on only two models, one of which (ChatTime) exhibits severe instruction-following/refusal behavior under the chosen prompt format. This confounds the claim that dedicated TSLMs broadly fall short, since poor performance may reflect prompt mismatch as much as architectural capability.

The VLM advantage may partly reflect plot-rendering conventions such as axes, gridlines, colors, and scaling rather than purely semantic time-series understanding. Robustness testing varies pixelation but not plotting style, leaving visual-encoding confounds only partially controlled.

Some claims are somewhat overstated. The 'first' benchmark framing overlaps with prior captioning benchmarks such as TADACap and CaTS-Bench, and the claim that all approaches are fragile is not uniformly supported, since amplitude scaling and some length perturbations leave performance largely stable.

The benchmark is limited to univariate time series, several datasets rely on synthetic or template-generated descriptions, and exact reproducibility is constrained by proprietary API models. The paper also states inconsistently whether code/data are already public or will be released upon acceptance.

Presentation has minor but noticeable issues: some table headings and modality labels appear garbled or misaligned, there are typos and inconsistent naming across the main text and appendix, which makes some results harder to parse than necessary.
